newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt's Mubarak discusses peace process with Levy.
newsitem.headline: Egypt's Mubarak discusses peace process with Levy.

text.p: pvs JERUSALEM)
By Mona Eltahawy

Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak held talks on Tuesday with Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy on a crisis in the Middle East peace process heightened by suicide bombings in Jerusalem last week and an Israeli clampdown on Palestinian self-rule areas.
Witnesses said Levy met Mubarak at a government house in Cairo known as the Al-Salam, or Peace, villa.

Middle East leaders are crisscrossing the region in search of a way out of the crisis in Israeli-PLO peacemaking, holding a series of meetings seen as a prelude to a visit to the region by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross expected later this week.

The Arab League's permanent members were meeting at their Cairo headquarters at the request of the Palestinians, after an Israeli crackdown on self-rule areas following the attacks in a Jerusalem market last Wednesday which killed 15, including the two bombers, and injured 170.

"The Palestinian Authority is a partner to the peace process and within this context we should deal with each other, especially when tragedies occur and our blood is shed," Levy told reporters at the airport before his talks with Mubarak.

"For this we expected from the Palestinian Authority to help us on security because without it there will be a terrorist eruption and terrorists will roam freely. We have taken precautionary measures not to weaken the Authority, but rather for awareness for security cooperation to eliminate terrorism."
"We are not imposing collective punishment..what we have done is only a small portion of what we can do," he said.

After the bombing, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called a halt to peace talks with the PLO and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, disrupting Palestinian trade and barring tens of thousands of Arab workers from reaching their workplaces in Israel.
Egypt's Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said at the airport, where he met Levy, that "It's no secret the peace process faces severe difficulties that it has never faced before."
In Amman, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat accused Netanyahu of wrecking the peace process and humiliating the Palestinians in the wake of the suicide bombings.
Arafat said Israel was exploiting the bombings to withdraw from its 1993 peace accords. The present Israeli government reluctantly inherited the accords from the previous Labour administration.

Arafat told reporters after talks with Prime Minister Abdul Salam al-Majali that his security bosses had told him that even Israeli intelligence pointed to the suicide bombers coming from outside Palestinian self-rule areas.

"We have been informed by military security officers that all their (Israeli) probabilities are that they (the bombers) have come from outside (self-rule areas), so what fault is this of the Palestinian people," Arafat said.
"So clearly the objective and aim is to wreck the peace process and the objective and aim is to humilitiate the Palestinian people," Arafat said angrily.
He urged the world community to act to save the peace process, describing it as a global accord which Israel had to respect.

"These accords are not bilateral, they are international, and I want to say now there is an international responsibility of all those who signed these accords to move to save the peace process from the crisis which Netanyahu is pushing daily," he added.
Arafat described Israel's sealing off of Palestinian self-rule areas as "...criminal measures, criminal, to starve the Palestinian people, to impose a siege on the people."
A senior Jordanian official said that in talks between Arafat and King Hussein, "they both stressed the importance of commitment to agreements signed between the two sides."
Officials said the king supported Arafat's view that the bombings were being exploited by Israel to backtrack on the peace accords.
Netanyahu will receive King Hussein on Wednesday, Netanyahu's office said on Monday.
Netanyahu was quoted on Sunday as saying that Israel would not honour peace deals it signed with Arafat unless the Palestinian Authority cracked down on Islamic militants.
On Monday Palestinian leaders called on the United Nations Security Council to protest against the actions on the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Syrian newspapers on Tuesday accused Netanyahu's government of creating a war-like atmosphere, saying there would be no peace until he left power or Israel changed its practices.
"The peace with Israel is in its (Syria's) interest and a continuation of a confrontational situation is certainly not a Syrian interest...

"Peace with Israel can give Syria very big gains as a country in the Middle East and as a country that wants to change its world standing," Netanyahu told reporters during a visit to an army induction centre near Tel Aviv.
